rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God lets rebels think they are escaping while his irresistible plan carries them toward destruction; its certainty needs no haste.
rows.anchor: His plans are bound to materialize and His grasp is inescapable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istidrāj is gradual deception, the greatest divine trial inflicted on those who rebel against God.
rows.anchor: The word إﺳﺘﺪرﺟﻪmeans to gradually be deceived. This is the greatest trial of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's familiar companion status means the Quraysh knew his character from childhood and every stage of life, making their charge of madness untenable.
rows.anchor: The word ﻢﺻﺎﺣﺒﻬ refers to Prophet Muḥammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He warns like a lookout because he sees danger ahead and loves his people; his urgency reflects awareness, while their lack of insight makes them call him mad.
rows.anchor: It is not madness but real awareness of the truth and profound love for his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh leaders did not truly believe the Prophet was mad; they found his certain warnings of punishment difficult to explain.
rows.anchor: In reality, the leaders of the Quraysh thought it strange that the Prophet (sws) warn them day and night of the punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To blunt his effect on ordinary people and preserve their political authority, Quraysh leaders spread the story that he was deluded.
rows.anchor: It was to do away with this impact and maintain their own political awe and authority that they floated this hoax

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an refutes the hoax by recalling his unmatched poise and stability: he is a mature, open warner, not a lunatic.
rows.anchor: He is the pinnacle of mental maturity and stability. He is not a lunatic; he is an open warner from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflecting on the cosmos shows that it is purposeful and must culminate in Judgment; the pure and upright succeed, while deviants become Hell’s fuel.
rows.anchor: this universe is not without a purpose; it is going to necessarily culminate on a day of judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each created thing manifests God’s power, mercy, wisdom, and providence and has an appointed term, so the world and its nations must also have an end and judgment.
rows.anchor: Whatever God has created is a manifestation of His power, mercy, wisdom and providence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only those who shut their eyes and ears and disregard reason can deny the testimony borne by the universe.
rows.anchor: This evidence borne by the collective system of the universe can only be denied by those who have closed their eyes and ears

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse suppresses the obvious conclusion that reflection would reveal the universe is purposeful; 3:191 states this conclusion explicitly.
rows.anchor: Thus in verse 191 of S ūrah Āl-i ‘Imr ān, it is said:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about their term drawing near is coordinated with the suppressed conclusion: reflection shows the purposeful universe has a fixed term.
rows.anchor: it would have become evident to them that this universe has a purpose and will exist until a certain prescribed time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflection should also show that the Quraysh’s respite is nearly over, as the Prophet warned.
rows.anchor: their own time of respite – which the Prophet (sws) was warning them of – has drawn near.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God seized earlier nations, he may seize the Quraysh for their misgivings; this corroborates Muhammad’s warning and shows that he is not mad.
rows.anchor: If He has seized other nations – whose history has been recounted earlier – why would He not seize the Quraysh for their misgivings?

rows.speaker: Ustādh Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī inclines to the second reading of “this”: the Qur’anic revelations whose denial produced the outcome.
rows.anchor: Ustādh Farāhī seems more inclined to the second of these views

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the first reading: “this” is the prescribed time previously mentioned, so the question asks what they will believe once their time expires.
rows.anchor: however, I am in favour of the first. In other words, the implied meaning is: what will they believe in when their time expires?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith must be accepted before the threatened event arrives; after it comes, the deniers will face its consequences.
rows.anchor: The time to accept faith is before their time expires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that none can guide those God leads astray intensifies the prior sorrow: they face God’s established practice and wander in rebellion beyond guidance.
rows.anchor: These people do not realize that they are facing an established practice of God and those who face it cannot be guided by anyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about when the Hour will arrive is sarcastic, as the contextual indications show.
rows.anchor: A question can be posed to make fun. Here, concomitant indications show that this precisely is the case here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-sāʿah means time here and covers both the worldly punishment warned of and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: here it refers to the time of punishment and to the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every messenger warns of worldly punishment for a rejecting nation and punishment in the Hereafter; deniers mock both, so al-sāʿah encompasses both.
rows.anchor: those who reject God’s Messengers make fun of both these punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about when it will arrive expresses amazement and improbability; the ship-anchoring term adds sarcasm, as if asking where the threatened ship is stuck.
rows.anchor: The sarcasm concealed in the question can well be gauged from this word.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual interpretation that the Day of Judgment is a heavy event in heaven and earth is a correct inference.
rows.anchor: have generally interpreted to mean that the Day of Judgement will be a heavy incident in the heavens and the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also pictures the Hour as a burden on the cosmos, like a pregnancy near delivery: its exact time is unknown, yet discerning observers see it is near and certain.
rows.anchor: this hour is a burden on the heavens and the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pregnant-woman analogy conveys that even without knowing the delivery time, a person can see that it is certain and near.
rows.anchor: yet every person with eyes can see and is certain that this woman will deliver the child and this will happen soon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those unable to see signs of Judgment in the heavens and earth resemble people unable to see a pregnant woman’s bulge near delivery.
rows.anchor: a subtle indication for those who are not able to see the signs of the Day of Judgement and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sudden arrival should prompt people to observe its signs.
rows.anchor: The part “will come upon you suddenly” implies that people should observe its signs of arrival

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship-anchoring term mursa conveys sarcasm, as though asking when the threatened ship will reach shore and anchor.
rows.anchor: When will it come to the shore to anchor?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyāna means “when” but is used here to ask in amazement and improbability.
rows.anchor: it is used when the purpose is to ask about something in order to express amazement and improbability about it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone truly knows the unseen; the Prophet’s affairs depend on God, and his revelation does not give him God’s authority or the keys to unseen knowledge.
rows.anchor: The implication of the verse is that true and real knower of the unseen is God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Prophet knew the unseen, he could gather abundant good and avoid harm; his actual afflictions show that he has no such knowledge, and his good is bounded by what he knows pleases God.
rows.anchor: Had he been given this knowledge, he would have gathered a lot treasure of all that is good and none would have been able to harm him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s lofty courage and desire mean he would leave no available good ungathered, though his knowledge of good is limited to his capacity and awareness.
rows.anchor: Such is the lofty status of a prophet with respect to his courage and desire that he does not want to leave out any good
